questions_and_answers.question_text: What must the verb chū be followed by?
What do the directional endings lái and qù add to the meaning?
What happens to the tones of lái and qù when used as directional endings?
What does the bound word jǐ- mean when unstressed, and when stressed?
What does the phrase following chūqu indicate?
What is the difference between chūqu and chūlai?

answers.answer_text: Chūqu corresponds to English "going out" (away from the speaker); chūlai to "coming out" (towards the speaker).

questions_and_answers.question_text: How do Chinese speakers often greet a friend, instead of saying "hello"?

answers.answer_text: They state the obvious — for example Nǐ lái le! ("You have come!"), Huílai le ("You're back"), or Nǐ yě dào zhèr lái le ("You have come here too").

questions_and_answers.question_text: How can you tell which jǐ- is being used?

answers.answer_text: Intonation and context will often help you decide.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "I thought I would go out to buy a few books."

answers.answer_text: Wǒ xiǎng chūqu mǎi jǐběn shū.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which verbs are often followed by purpose expressions?

articles.text:
1. B: Nǐ chūqu a!                    Oh, you're going out!
   A: Wǒ xiǎng chūqu mǎi jǐběn      I thought I would go out to buy a
      shū.                          few books.

Notes on No. 1

Chūqu, "to go out (away from the speaker)": The verb chū means "to go/come out," "to exit," in the sense of leaving an area. Chū must be followed either by the name of the place being left (as in chūle zhèige fàndiàn) or by the verb lái or qù used as a DIRECTIONAL ENDING. When lái or qù follows, the verb indicates not only that the person exits but also that the person exits towards or away from the speaker. Chūqu corresponds to the English "going out," and chūlai to "coming out."

Tā zǎoshang jiù chūqu le.        He went out this morning.
Tā zài nèige shāngdiànli mǎi     He has been in that shop buying
cài yǐjing sānshifēn zhōng       groceries for thirty minutes
le! Hái méi chūlai!              already, and he hasn't come
                                 out yet!

When the verbs lái and qù are used as directional endings, they are unstressed and toneless.

Nǐ chūqu a! Sometimes this expression might be used as a greeting. Instead of saying "hello" when greeting a friend or acquaintance, the Chinese state the obvious. For example, if you (Ān Dàwéi) drop in unexpectedly on a Chinese friend, probably the first thing he will say is O! Ān Dàwéi! Nǐ lái le! Qǐng jìn, "Oh! Ān Dàwéi! You have come! Please come in." Or if you run an errand and then return, you will probably be greeted with Huílai le, "You're back." A friend of yours who runs into you downtown may say Nǐ yě dào zhèr lái le, "You have come here too." In Chinese these remarks are a common form of greeting.

Jǐběn: The bound word jǐ- means "a few." It is unstressed and often toneless. When stressed, jǐ- is the question word "how many."

Tā mǎile jǐběn shū.              He bought a few books.
Tā mǎile jǐběn shū?              How many books did he buy?

Intonation and context will often help you decide which jǐ- is being used.

Chūqu mǎi jǐběn shū: The phrase following the verb chūqu indicates the purpose of going out. Purpose expressions often follow the verbs lái, qù, and their compounds.
